title: JSON Schema for Published REST Operation
reason: Describes the generated JSON schema rules for published REST operation request and response bodies, which developers still need when documenting or consuming these services.
summary: Explains how Mendix derives the OpenAPI/JSON Schema for published REST operations from import and export mappings based on message definitions. Covers the definition naming rule, attribute-to-schema type mapping, and how object, list, file and primitive results are represented.
key_facts: Schemas are generated only for import/export mappings based on message definitions; otherwise the body or result is typed as file.
The definition name defaults to the message definition name and can be overridden by setting the public name of the mapping.
Autonumber and Long map to integer/int64, Integer maps to integer/int32, Decimal to number, Boolean to boolean, and Date and time to string/date-time.
Enumeration attributes map to a string schema with an enum list; Binary maps to string/binary.
Object results reference a definition via $ref; list results are type array with items referencing the definition.
Primitive results: Boolean and Decimal and Integer/Long have direct schemas, while String, Binary, Date and time and Enumeration results are typed as file.

title: Consumed REST Service
reason: Current Mendix reference for building, testing and using Consumed REST Service documents, still actionable for REST integration work.
summary: The Consumed REST Service document lets developers configure GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests in Studio Pro, test them, and generate domain model entities from JSON responses or bodies. Several limits apply, notably that only 200 responses can be mapped directly in microflows and non-JSON responses need manual extraction.
key_facts: Only responses with status code 200 can be mapped in a microflow; for other 2xx codes use latestHttpResponse to read StatusCode and Content.
Automatic entity creation from a response requires the response to be JSON; XML or raw text must be parsed in a microflow.
Parameters are supported in the URL path, query, header values and body, but not in the Authentication section or the Query Parameters table.
Basic authentication credentials should be stored in constants; other auth types must be added as custom headers.
Streaming responses from APIs are not supported.
Consumed REST Service is GA on Windows only; macOS support is still beta, and OpenAPI/Swagger import is beta.

title: Password Policy
reason: Describes current Mendix password policy settings that developers configure and rely on when securing apps.
summary: Mendix password policy, set in App Security under the Password policy tab, is enforced when creating users or changing passwords. It offers four requirements: minimum length, digit, mixed case, and symbol.
key_facts: Password policy is set in App Security > Password policy tab.
Policy applies when creating new users or changing existing user passwords.
Minimum length sets the minimum number of characters in a password.
Require digit: at least one digit is required.
Require mixed case: at least one lowercase and one uppercase character is required.
Require symbol: at least one of ` ~ ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) - _ = + [ { ] } \ is required.

title: Technical Details of Published REST
reason: The page is only a list of links to other reference pages and contains no practitioner knowledge of its own.
summary: This index page lists the technical reference pages for Published REST in Mendix Studio Pro, covering routing, JSON schema, OpenAPI 2.0 and 3.0 documents, and the custom authentication microflow parameters. It contains no operational guidance itself.

title: Published REST Service
reason: Configuration reference that developers act on when publishing REST services, covering auth methods, CSRF, reserved URL prefixes and custom authentication behaviour.
summary: Explains how to configure a published REST service in Studio Pro: naming and location, authentication methods (basic, active session, custom microflow), and allowed roles. Also covers the order in which authentication methods are tried and how the custom authentication microflow's result is handled.
key_facts: Default location is rest/<service name>/v1; invalid URL characters in the service name are stripped or replaced with _.
The URL prefixes api-doc/, xas/, p/ and reload/ are reserved and cannot start a service location.
With several authentication methods checked, Studio Pro tries Custom first, then Username and password, then Active session.
Active session authentication cannot be used by offline-first apps, and state-changing requests need the X-Csrf-Token header.
A custom authentication microflow returns a User: a non-empty User runs the operation as that user, an empty User moves on to the next method, and a non-200 HttpResponse status is returned directly.
Web service users cannot access published REST services; allowed roles require Requires authentication to be set to Yes.

title: REST Services
reason: Current reference on Mendix REST services; a practitioner would still use it to find the right consume/publish and mapping docs.
summary: Explains Mendix REST fundamentals: URLs, headers and HTTP methods, content types for JSON, and how JSON structures, import mappings and export mappings convert between JSON/XML and Mendix objects. Lists the related docs for publishing and consuming REST services.
key_facts: REST uses HTTP URLs to locate resources, HTTP headers for authentication and content type, and HTTP methods such as GET and POST for operations.
REST calls that output JSON must declare the content type as application/JSON.
Content types are passed in custom HTTP headers on the call to specify output media type or data format.
A JSON Structure is extracted from an example JSON snippet and used in Mapping Documents.
Import Mapping converts JSON or XML to Mendix objects; Export Mapping serializes Mendix objects to JSON or XML.
Publishing uses Published REST Services and HttpRequest/HttpResponse system entities; consuming uses Consumed REST Service and the Call REST Service microflow action.

title: Published REST Services
reason: Practical reference on securing and exposing published REST services, including authentication options and API documentation; still relevant as current product guidance.
summary: Explains how to expose entities and microflows as published REST services and which authentication options apply (basic, active session, none, anonymous, custom microflow). It also covers the auto-generated Swagger/OpenAPI documentation and how to enable trace logging for REST publish.
key_facts: Basic and active session authentication are default when app security level is Prototype/demo or Production.
Anonymous access to a published REST service requires anonymous user in allowed roles and Username and password as authentication method.
Web service users cannot access REST services.
Each published service is documented in Swagger UI under /rest-doc/ and in OpenAPI 3.0 and 2.0 formats.
Set the REST Publish log node to Trace for detailed interaction logging.

title: Module Security
reason: Current Mendix reference on module roles and access matrices (page, microflow, entity, REST, OData), directly relevant to app security practice.
summary: Module security in Mendix defines module roles and access matrices for pages, microflows, nanoflows, entities, OData/GraphQL and REST services, plus dataset access. Page access alone does not restrict navigation, so entity and microflow access rules must enforce real restrictions.
key_facts: Page access only hides pages from navigation and buttons; deeplinks can still reach them, so enforce restrictions with entity and microflow access.
Microflow allowed roles are checked only when the microflow is executed from the client; a microflow calling another microflow skips the check.
Entity access grants Create, Read, Write and Delete per module role and can carry an XPath constraint.
The REST Access tab appears only when the published REST service requires authentication.
Module role names are not shown to end users; they see user role names only.
Dataset access is Full, Limited or No access per module role, governed by parameter constraints and ranges.

title: Generating a Published REST Resource
reason: Describes a concrete, still-current Mendix procedure for generating REST resources and the operations, microflows, mappings it creates.
summary: Publishing an entity as a REST resource generates a resource, selected operations, a microflow per operation, a message definition, and import/export mappings. Existing message definitions and mappings are reused rather than duplicated.
key_facts: Expose as REST resource via right-click on an entity in the domain model, or drag an entity or message definition onto a published REST service's resource list.
Get by key, Patch and Delete require a unique key attribute on the entity.
Operations: Get all, Get by key, Post, Patch, Delete.
Import mappings are created for Post and Patch; export mappings for Get all and Get by key.
An existing message definition for the entity is reused, along with its existing import and export mappings.

title: Custom Authentication Microflow Parameters
reason: Describes how to define microflow parameters for published REST authentication, a current practitioner setup step.
summary: The custom authentication microflow of a published REST service receives values from request headers or query parameters, which must each be declared as parameters and mapped to a microflow parameter. Only primitive data types are supported.
key_facts: Declare every microflow parameter in the Authentication microflow arguments dialog (Parameters next to the authentication microflow).
Parameter type Header takes the value of the first request header with the given name.
Parameter type Query takes the value from the query string, e.g. ?name=John.
Set the Name to the request header name for header parameters.
Only primitive data types are supported.
Always select a Microflow Parameter to receive the value.

title: Recommendations from Best Practice Recommender
reason: Actionable Mendix performance rules with specific fixes that developers still apply when building and reviewing apps.
summary: Lists the Best Practice Recommender performance checks (MXP001 to MXP010 and beyond) and how to fix each one, covering calculated attributes, indexes, commit batching, nanoflow conversion, caching and inheritance depth. The page is truncated before the access-rule guidance ends.
key_facts: Avoid calculated attributes on pages (MXP001) and remove unused calculated attributes (MXP002), because retrieving an object runs their microflow logic.
Add indexes to attributes used in sort orders on read-intensive entities (MXP003), and to attributes used in XPath expressions when the entity holds at least about 10,000 records (MXP007).
Do not commit inside a loop (MXP004/MXP005). Set Commit to No, collect objects in a list, and commit after the loop or every 1000 objects.

Convert eligible microflows to nanoflows (MXP006), but only if they avoid most database actions and do not use $latestSoapFault, $latestHttpResponse, $currentSession, $currentUser or $currentDeviceType.
Do not cache non-persistable entities (MXP008). Cache data only when it changes rarely, is read often, is limited in volume (under about 10,000 records) and stale data is acceptable.
Limit inheritance to two levels (MXP009) and avoid duplicated entity access rules (MXP010), especially XPath-based ones.

title: CORS Settings for Published REST Services
reason: Concise reference for configuring CORS on published REST services, still relevant for securing REST endpoints.
summary: CORS settings on a Mendix published REST service control which origins may call it from a browser, how long browsers cache those rules, and whether cookies or auth headers may be sent. Use a comma-separated constant of origins, or `*` only for public services that need no authentication.
key_facts: Allowed Origins is a constant holding a comma-separated list of origins (protocol + hostname + optional port), e.g. https://www.mendix.com or http://example.com:8080.
Use the value `*` only for public services that are accessible from any origin and do not require authentication.
Max Age sets how long browsers cache CORS settings; longer values reduce preflight requests but delay propagation of changes.
Allow Credentials permits the browser to send cookies, authorization headers and/or client certificates to the service.
CORS is configured per published REST service and is enabled there.

title: Version a REST Service
reason: Gives actionable Mendix guidance on versioning published REST services, including when to bump MAJOR, MINOR or PATCH and how to deprecate old versions.
summary: Publish breaking REST service changes as a new major version by duplicating the service and its microflows, mappings and message definitions, never editing a live service. Mark the old version as deprecated, document the replacement, and notify users before eventually removing it.
key_facts: Use MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: a new MAJOR for incompatible changes such as removing an operation, MINOR for backwards-compatible additions, PATCH for backwards-compatible bug fixes.
Do not change a published service that clients use; duplicate the service and give it a new version instead.
Put each service version's microflows, mappings and message definitions in a folder named ServiceName_Version.
Duplicate only what changed; the new version reuses unchanged microflows, mappings and message definitions from the previous version.
Deprecate by adding (deprecated) to the service name, describing the reason and new version in Public documentation, and marking changed operations as deprecated.
Omit .0 from version segments in URLs, for example rest/myservice/v1.1.

title: Strict Mode
reason: Explains a production security safety net for Mendix React apps, including which client APIs are blocked and the workarounds developers need today.
summary: Strict mode, enabled in App Security with the React client and Production security level, blocks client-side data APIs so entities are only changed through microflows, nanoflows, widgets, or pages. Developers must move JavaScript-action data changes to nanoflows and use workarounds for File Uploader delete and Web Actions take-picture.
key_facts: Enable strict mode in App Security only when the React client is enabled and the security level is Production.
Strict mode restricts data.action, data.create, data.commit, data.remove, data.rollback, and data.get (GUID and GUIDs remain allowed).
Restricted APIs are disabled at runtime, so they cannot be called from JavaScript actions or the browser console in online apps.
Use a nanoflow instead of a JavaScript action when a data change is needed.
File Uploader delete does not work in strict mode; use a custom button that calls a nanoflow to delete the file object.
Save and Cancel Changes actions must sit in editable widgets or snippets, not directly in layouts, or Studio Pro raises a consistency error.

title: Operation Parameters for Published REST
reason: Describes how to configure published REST operation parameters (query, path, body, header, form) and mapping behavior, which practitioners still need when building REST services.
summary: Explains the settings for published REST operation parameters: where each parameter type comes from, how body parameters map through import mappings, and how find-miss and commit behavior are configured. Use it when adding or editing parameters on a published REST operation.
key_facts: Parameter types: Query, Path, Body, Header, Form; object or list parameters can only come from the body.
A microflow can have 0 or 1 body parameter; GET, HEAD and OPTIONS operations should not have body parameters.
Header parameter names must match the request header; Authorization and other OpenAPI-reserved names can conflict in Swagger UI (not the real endpoint).
'If no object was found' options are Create, Ignore or Error, and apply only when the import mapping has 'Decide this at the place where the mapping gets used' checked.
Commit options: Yes (triggers events and validation), Yes without events, or No (commit manually in the microflow).
Primitive import mappings work only if the operation has at most one path parameter of that type.

title: HttpRequest and HttpResponse System Entities
reason: Documents the HttpRequest and HttpResponse system entities that developers use when publishing or consuming REST services, including a non-obvious ReasonPhrase limitation.
summary: HttpRequest and HttpResponse are system entities for handling REST requests and responses, with headers managed through the HttpHeaders association. Setting ReasonPhrase has no effect because Mendix Runtime's web server only uses the default phrase for each status code, so it is effectively read-only.
key_facts: HttpRequest exposes Uri (full URI including query parameters) and Content (request body); headers are read through the HttpHeaders association.
HttpResponse has StatusCode (Integer, default 200), ReasonPhrase (default OK) and Content (response body).
Response headers are retrieved or created through HttpResponse's HttpHeaders association, each HttpHeader having Key and Value.
Set Content-Type on the response to tell the client how to interpret the body.
Setting ReasonPhrase has no effect in Mendix Runtime; treat it as read-only.
HttpVersion defaults to HTTP/1.1 and can almost always be ignored.

title: Publish a REST Service
reason: Practical, current how-to for publishing a native Mendix REST service with operations, microflow, export mapping, and error handling, still actionable today.
summary: Shows how to publish a REST GET operation in Studio Pro using a message definition, a published REST service with a path parameter, and a microflow that retrieves an order and returns JSON via export mapping. It also covers building an HttpResponse with headers and adding error handling that returns a 400-style JSON error for invalid IDs.
key_facts: Create a message definition (MD_...) selecting the entity and its attributes, including attributes from associations, before building the service.
Use a path parameter like {OrderID} in the operation path; the microflow parameter must match it.
Convert the String OrderID to Integer/Long before retrieving, because AutoNumber attributes need an integer match.
Remove any automatically added httpRequest parameter; remove an automatically added httpResponse parameter if using an export mapping (error CE0346 otherwise).

Build an HttpResponse with StatusCode, Content and HttpVersion, plus an HttpHeader with Key 'Content-Type' and Value 'application/json', linked via System.HttpHeaders; return $NewHttpResponse from the End Event.
Export with mapping is optional: published services support content negotiation, so returning a list from the microflow is also possible.

title: Anonymous Users
reason: Describes how to configure anonymous users and restrict their access, which a developer would still act on today.
summary: Anonymous users let end-users use an app without signing in, and the app assigns them a specific user role that controls what they can see. Mendix advises naming that role `Anonymous` and restricting it with entity and microflow access rules.
key_facts: Enable anonymous users under App Security > Anonymous users by setting 'Allow anonymous users' to Yes.
Select an 'Anonymous user role' only after 'Allow anonymous users' is set to Yes.
Name the anonymous user role 'Anonymous' so its purpose is clear.
Anonymous access exposes the app to anyone, so limit the anonymous role with entity and microflow access rules.
See 'Configuring User Roles and Access' in Implement Best Practices for App Security for further guidance.

title: App Security
reason: Describes current Mendix app-level security settings and security levels that developers must configure before production, which remains actionable.
summary: App Security in Mendix Studio Pro sets the app's security level (Off, Prototype/demo, Production) and the related settings such as user roles, administrator, demo users, anonymous users and password policy. Security must be switched on at app level before module security and entity access rules can be configured.
key_facts: Security levels are Off, Prototype/demo and Production; Production applies full security to signing in, forms, microflows, entities and reports.
Licensed Mendix Cloud nodes must use the Production security level and configure all security settings.
Off and Prototype/demo levels are only allowed for local testing, Free Apps, or non-Mendix Cloud Development mode environments.
Enable Strict page URL checking so pages reachable only by URL get the same security consistency checks; it is enabled by default in new apps.
Check Security (Production only) validates that forms and referenced attributes/associations are accessible per user role and reports errors in the error list.
App status is Complete only when all security settings for the current level are configured; check the Module Status tab for what remains.

title: Security
reason: Current Mendix security overview covering team, app/module security, roles, authentication options; practitioners still act on it.
summary: Mendix security is handled in three layers: team access managed in Projects, end-user access configured in Studio Pro via app and module security, and authentication chosen as local, Mendix SSO, or a third-party IdP. A module's own roles are combined into app-level user roles that determine what end-users can reach at runtime.
key_facts: With production security on, nothing is accessible by default; forms, entities, microflows and workflows must be explicitly granted.
User roles are app-level and are built from module roles; a user gets the access of all their user roles.
Always include System.User in the user roles, since it is required.
Entity access uses XPath constraints and member-level read/write rules; document access applies to pages, microflows and OData.
Authentication options: local (Administration module, optional MFA modules), Mendix SSO (default for Mendix Cloud), or third-party IdP via SAML 2.0, OIDC, or SAP XSUAA.
Since Studio Pro 11, the ShowHomePage microflow enforces entity access by default.

title: Use Call REST Service Action in a Microflow
reason: Gives a repeatable procedure for calling a REST service from a microflow with URL parameters and an import mapping, which developers still use.
summary: Shows how to consume a REST service from a microflow by creating a JSON structure, generating an import mapping from it, and calling the service with the Call REST service action. The result is stored in an entity and displayed on a page.
key_facts: Create the JSON structure from a sample response (paste the JSON, click Refresh), then generate entities with Import Mapping > Map automatically.
Use a non-persistable input entity as the microflow parameter and pass its attribute into the URL template as {1}, e.g. .../summary/{1} with $Input/Title.
In the Call REST service action's Response tab, set Response handling to Apply import mapping and store the output in a variable.
To link the result to the input object, use a Change object activity that sets the association member to the stored variable.
Set Refresh in client to Yes on the Change object activity so the page shows the result.
The example uses an unauthenticated GET request, so no credentials are needed.

title: Published REST Request Routing
reason: Useful as an index to REST request routing and the 400/401/404/405 causes, but the substantive answers are in a flowchart image that isn't in the text.
summary: The page explains how the server routes an incoming REST request to a published operation microflow and which security applies. It covers the outcomes for 400, 401, 404 and 405 responses, but the routing logic itself is only in an image.
key_facts: The example request GET /rest/petstore/pet/12 is used to illustrate routing.
Routing determines which published REST operation microflow runs for a URL.
Routing also determines which security (basic or anonymous authentication) applies to the request.
The page covers 400 Bad Request, 401 Not Authorized, 404 Not Found and 405 Method Not Allowed responses.
Exception and empty HttpResponse behaviour in operation microflows is covered by the flowchart.

title: Antivirus Exclusion
reason: Practical setup guidance for antivirus exclusions that affect Studio Pro performance, still applicable to current Studio Pro versions.
summary: Studio Pro can slow down under antivirus scanning, so exclude the app folder (not studiopro.exe) from Microsoft Defender or your antivirus. The exclusion notification can be turned off in Preferences if needed.
key_facts: Add the app folder, or the folder containing all apps, to antivirus exclusions; this requires administrator privileges.
Do not add studiopro.exe itself to ignored processes; Studio Pro subprocesses and tools are not covered by excluding only the executable.
Only exclude app directories you trust.
Studio Pro does not verify that antivirus is actually active in the folder; the notification only indicates antivirus software is running.
To disable the notification: Edit > Preferences > Advanced, then check 'Do not show antivirus exclusion notifications'.

title: Community Best Practices for App Performance
reason: Recent, concrete Mendix performance guidance on indexes, loops, commits, XPath and domain model design that developers still act on.
summary: Community guidance for Mendix app performance covering domain model design, indexes, microflow loops and batching, XPath rewrites, pages, and moving long-running work off the user's path. It favours simple designs first and measuring before optimising.
key_facts: Create indexes on entities expected to exceed 100 records that are searched by attributes other than Mendix IDs; keep index attributes below three, and never more than five.
Avoid 'not' and 'unequal' in XPath; rewrite as positive constraints such as boolean = false() or enumeration = valueA.
Retrieving a list and counting it is optimised by Mendix into a single query, so retrieve again later only when the data is needed.
Commit and delete after the loop using a commit list, or in batches driven by a counter, and clear the commit list after each commit; commit as late as possible to limit record locking.
Minimise calculated attributes, event handlers and reference sets, because they run on every retrieve, commit or row.
Run work the user does not wait for (mail, external interface updates) asynchronously, using a task queue or background microflows from Community Commons.

title: User Roles
reason: Current Mendix reference on user role design, module role aggregation and user management rules that practitioners still act on.
summary: User roles bundle module roles and are assigned to end-users; they should be changed with care because edits only apply after users sign out and back in. User management settings control which roles a user role can grant or revoke.
key_facts: A user role is made of one or more module roles; a typical user role includes System.User plus at least one other module role.
Keep module roles separate from user roles so modules stay reusable and Marketplace-publishable.
Changes to user roles do not apply immediately to signed-in users; advise end-users to sign out and back in.
Do not use user role changes to build dynamic UI, since they do not take effect immediately.
Manageable roles define which end-user roles a user role can grant or remove; a manager with an unselected role cannot manage that user.
User management settings become implicit entity access rules on System.User and are not enforced when a microflow runs with Apply entity access enabled.

title: Security Overview
reason: Explains how to review an app's effective runtime access per user role, which a developer would use on any Mendix project today.
summary: The Security Overview shows what each user role can actually access at runtime: entities, attributes, associations, pages, microflows and nanoflows. Combined access rules are aggregated, so any rule that grants access makes it effective, and the results can be exported to Excel or via the mx CLI for review.
key_facts: The Security Overview is only available when the app's security level is set to Production.
Combined access rules are aggregated: if any rule grants access, the role has it, e.g. Read+Create plus ReadWrite gives ReadWrite and Create.
Entities with XPath constraints appear in separate columns; rules with the same XPath are combined.
Attributes, associations and entities the selected role cannot access are not shown.
Export to Excel produces sheets for members access, entity access, document access and module roles; the mx CLI command export-security-overview exports JSON or xlsx.
Selecting a module filters the Entity, Page, Microflow and Nanoflow tabs; the System module and protected modules are not listed.

title: Demo Users
reason: Describes how demo users are created, enabled and used to test each user role, which a Mendix developer still acts on for role testing.
summary: Demo users are auto-created per user role when the app starts locally or on a Free App, and they can be used to switch between roles for testing or demos. They are regular local users, so disabling the feature does not remove or block them.
key_facts: Demo users are created automatically on first start and only appear when running locally or in a Free App environment.
Enable demo users = Yes allows creating, editing and deleting demo users; No blocks those changes.
Disabling demo users does not delete them or block sign-in; they remain ordinary local users with their passwords.
Demo user names must be unique and cannot equal the administrator user name.
A demo user's entity must be System.User or a specialization, and it needs at least one user role.
Test roles by signing in as Administrator and selecting a demo user from the Select user menu.

title: Administrator
reason: Describes current Mendix Administrator account defaults and password-change caveats that a developer would still act on when securing an app.
summary: The default MxAdmin administrator account (password 1, role Administrator) should be renamed and given a custom password before go-live. Changing the admin password in the model does not affect cloud environments, which must be changed in the Mendix Portal.
key_facts: Default administrator user name is MxAdmin; change it to a custom name because the default is common knowledge.
Default administrator password is 1; replace it with a custom password.
The model password only applies when running locally; cloud environments must be changed in the Mendix Portal (Environment Details).
Administrator user role defaults to Administrator (System.Administrator module role) and can manage all manageable roles.
In cloud deployments, a change to the admin user role is not applied until the admin password is changed.
Free Apps do not create MxAdmin automatically; it is created when the password is first changed in a licensed environment.

title: Publish and Retrieve Images and Files with REST
reason: Practical, current guidance for publishing and consuming binary files over REST in Mendix, with concrete steps and content-type settings a developer would still act on.
summary: Publish System.Image or System.FileDocument entities as a REST service to expose binary file content, and set the Content-Type header in the GET microflow so clients render the file correctly. Retrieve remote files into a FileDocument-derived entity via the Call REST service action, the Image widget, or an HTML embed.
key_facts: Generalize the entity from System.Image or System.FileDocument, then use Expose as a REST resource and select the key attribute with Get all, Get by key, Post and Delete operations.

By default a Get by key with no export mapping returns raw binary content; set a Content-Type header via a System.HTTPHeader Create Object action with Key 'Content-Type' and Value e.g. 'image/png' or 'application/pdf', assigned to $httpResponse, before the End event.
Test via the OpenAPI document link or the VS Code REST Client with an Accept header matching the file type.
To consume files, call the REST service with the Call REST service action, set Response handling to Store in a file document, and store the result in a RetrievedFile entity.
For images, add a Change object action afterwards with Refresh in client set to Yes so the image viewer updates.
Use the Image widget (Image URL source) for images and the HTMLSnippet widget with an embed tag for PDFs; both require the Marketplace widget to be imported.

title: Published REST Path Parameters
reason: Concrete, still-applicable rules for defining path parameters on published REST operations in Mendix.
summary: Path parameters in a published REST operation's path capture URL segments as microflow or import mapping parameters. They must be primitive types, appear between slashes, and cannot be repeated or contain curly braces.
key_facts: Specify path parameters in the operation path between { and }.
Do not use the same path parameter twice in one operation path.
Parameter names cannot contain curly braces.
Path parameters must be primitive: Boolean, date and time, decimal, enumeration, integer/long, or string.
Path parameters can only appear between slashes in the path.
Generated microflows create string parameters for path parameters; change the type in the microflow if needed. Date and time values use ISO-8601, e.g. 2018-12-31T09:00:00.

title: Published REST Operation
reason: Durable reference on Mendix published REST operation configuration, method semantics, parameters, and response handling that developers still act on.
summary: A published REST operation maps an HTTP method and path under a published resource to a microflow, with parameters, import/export mappings and response handling defined on it. Responses depend on the microflow return type and Content-Type/Accept negotiation.
key_facts: Supported methods: GET, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; GET, HEAD and DELETE have no body parameter.
Path parameters are written between { and } in the operation path and are passed to the microflow or import mapping.
Object or List body parameters need an import mapping; FileDocument parameters do not.
A non-empty primitive return value is used as the response body and the HttpResponse Content is ignored; never return an empty HttpResponse.
If the export mapping supports XML and JSON, the format follows the microflow's Content-Type header, else the Accept header, defaulting to JSON.
When security is enabled, the microflow needs at least one role configured to be accessible; an unhandled exception returns 500.

title: Server-Side Paging and Sorting for a Microflow Data Source
reason: Practical, current how-to for server-side paging, sorting and searching on a microflow data source fed by a REST call, with concrete template and parameter expressions a developer would reuse.
summary: Explains how to make a microflow data source for a data grid page through its REST call, so the grid fetches only one page and sorts on the server. It covers the Paging parameter, the REST template placeholders for page, sort attribute and order, and setting a default sort or disabling sorting.
key_facts: Use the generated Paging object's PageNumber in the REST Call template via {1} with the parameter toString($Paging/PageNumber).
Pass sort attribute and direction with parameters toLowerCase($Paging/SortAttribute) and if $Paging/SortAscending then 'asc' else 'desc' mapped to {2} and {3}.
Generate controls when prompted to enable server-side paging, sorting and searching; this adds the Paging input to the microflow.
Set a default sort by adding a Create object activity in the data view's Go to data source nanoflow setting Paging SortAttribute.
To disable header sorting for REST services without sort support, set Paging IsSortable to false in the data source nanoflow.
The data grid is a Dojo widget, so the runtime setting Use React client must be No to see it in the Toolbox.

title: Published REST Query Parameters
reason: Concrete, still-applicable rules for handling query parameters in published REST operations that developers act on when building endpoints.
summary: Query parameters on a published REST operation must be primitive types and are read from the query string after a question mark. Missing parameters arrive as empty in the microflow, except Boolean parameters, which default to false.
key_facts: Query parameters must be a primitive type: Boolean, date and time, decimal, enumeration, integer/long, or string.
Query parameter names are case sensitive.
Pass query parameters after a question mark, for example ?name=John&age=42.
Date and time parameters must use ISO-8601 format, for example 2018-12-31T09:00:00.
If a client omits a query parameter, the microflow receives empty, except Boolean parameters, which receive false.

title: Manage App Performance with New Relic
reason: Describes how to set up New Relic Java agent for Mendix on-premises and Cloud Foundry, which is still actionable for performance monitoring.
summary: Setting up New Relic APM for a Mendix app means adding the New Relic Java agent via -javaagent in the JVM options, either in m2ee.yaml javaopts, Studio Pro's Extra JVM parameters, or the Cloud Foundry buildpack. Once enabled, requests and database calls appear in New Relic's transaction and database views.
key_facts: New Relic is not supported for apps deployed to Mendix Cloud.
On-premises: download the Java agent archive from New Relic and put the license key in newrelic.yml.
Linux/Windows service console: add "-javaagent:<path>/javaagent.jar" to the javaopts list in m2ee.yaml.
Studio Pro (development mode only): add -javaagent:<path>/javaagent.jar to Extra JVM parameters on the Server tab of a configuration.
Cloud Foundry: follow the cf-mendix-buildpack New Relic instructions.
After setup, requests appear under Transactions and database calls under Databases.

title: Detect and Resolve Performance Issues
reason: Practical, current Mendix guidance on diagnosing and fixing slow UI, microflows, retrieves and commits that practitioners would still act on.
summary: Shows how to tell a UI-centric slowdown from a microflow-centric one, then time microflows and activities to locate the slow part. Gives fixes for slow retrieves, commits, loops and large batches.
key_facts: Use browser developer tools to tell too many UI loads from slow individual loads.
Time microflows with a Create variable / Log message pair, or with TimeMeasureStart and TimeMeasureEnd from Community Commons; every TimeMeasureStart needs a matching TimeMeasureEnd.
Set the LogMinDurationQuery custom setting (for example 500 ms) to log slow OQL and XPath queries and commits.
Commit lists once after a loop instead of committing inside it by setting Commit to No on each change activity.
Turn off Refresh in client for large commits, since it updates values in the browser and can cascade through nested data views.
Run big operations asynchronously and batch them to avoid memory growth, for example with commit lists above about 10k objects.

title: Integrate a Legacy System into a Mendix App
reason: Gives a practitioner a concrete, repeatable procedure for consuming a REST service with the Mendix REST module, mapping JSON into domain models and displaying results.
summary: Shows how to integrate a legacy system exposed as a REST/JSON service into a Mendix app by modelling the JSON response, calling it with the REST GET action from a microflow, and mapping the results into domain objects for display. The worked example uses the Google Books API, and the same pattern extends to POST and other data sources.
key_facts: Model the JSON response as Mendix JSON structures first; each REST service has its own structure.
Use a non-persistable search entity and a data view to collect user input.
Call the REST GET Java action from a microflow and map the response into persistent result objects.
Retrieve nested associations (for example, an author list) per item and iterate over them to build display data.
Use the REST POST action to push values from Mendix to an external system.

title: OpenAPI 2.0 Documentation
reason: Vendor reference describing what Mendix generates in swagger.json; useful for client generation and testing but largely restates product documentation.
summary: Every published Mendix REST service generates an OpenAPI 2.0 swagger.json, downloadable from /rest-doc/{location}/swagger.json or exported from Studio Pro. The document maps which service, resource and operation settings populate the file's info, paths, tags, security and body parameters.
key_facts: swagger.json is downloadable from /rest-doc/{location}/swagger.json, where {location} is e.g. rest/myservice/v1, or exported from Studio Pro.
info.version is always 1.0.0; basePath is /rest/servicename.
Each resource becomes a tag using its name and public documentation.
A body parameter is generated only for POST, PUT, PATCH and OPTIONS operations.
When security is enabled, basic authentication is added to securityDefinitions and security, and an unauthorized response is added to operations.
Operations marked deprecated are emitted with deprecated set to true.

title: Publishing a Microflow as a REST Operation
reason: Explains a concrete, still-current Studio Pro procedure for publishing a microflow as a REST operation, including a constraint that causes consistency errors.
summary: Publish a microflow as a REST operation by right-clicking it in the microflow editor and choosing a service and resource, then adjust the operation. The microflow cannot be published if it takes more than one object or list parameter.
key_facts: Right-click in the microflow editor and select 'Publish as REST service operation'.
A microflow with more than one parameter of object or list type cannot be published and raises a consistency error.
Choose an existing service and resource, create a new resource in an existing service, or create a new service in a module or folder.
The suggested resource name is the entity of a parameter or the entity result of the microflow.
Suggested HTTP method is POST when the microflow takes an object or list parameter, otherwise GET.

title: OpenAPI 3.0 Documentation
reason: Reference material on the openapi.json generated for published REST services, useful when consuming or documenting a service but mostly descriptive.
summary: Every published REST service automatically gets an OpenAPI 3.0 openapi.json, which can be exported from Studio Pro or downloaded from /rest-doc/{location}/openapi.json. The page maps each part of the file (info, servers, paths, components, security, tags) to the service, resource and operation settings that generate it.
key_facts: Download the spec from /rest-doc/{location}/openapi.json, for example rest/myservice/v1, or export it from Studio Pro.
info.version is always 1.0.0; info.title and info.description come from the service name and public documentation.
servers contains the base URL the app runs on.
With security enabled, components.securitySchemes, security and the unauthorized response add basic authentication.
requestBody is generated for POST, PUT and PATCH; path, query and header parameters are generated from the operation.
An operation marked deprecated gets deprecated: true in the spec.
